listeningScripts.title: Booking Driving Lessons
listeningScripts.text:
Instructor: Hello, Callaghan Driving School.
Caller: Hi, I'd like to book some lessons. I've just got my provisional licence.
Instructor: Congratulations. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Rosalind Pemberton. Pemberton is P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N.
Instructor: And a mobile number?
Caller: 07729 486 315.
Instructor: Have you driven at all before?
Caller: Only on a private track, a couple of times.
Instructor: That's useful but it doesn't count for much on the road. I'd start you at the beginning either way.
Caller: How long are the lessons?
Instructor: Two hours is standard. I know an hour sounds easier to fit in, but by the time you've driven somewhere quiet and settled, half of it has gone.
Caller: Two hours then. What does it cost?
Instructor: Thirty-four pounds an hour, so sixty-eight a lesson. If you buy a block of ten it comes down to thirty-one an hour.
Caller: I'll take the block. How many will I need altogether?
Instructor: The honest answer is that the average is around forty-five hours with an instructor, plus private practice. Anyone promising a pass in ten is selling you something.
Caller: That's more than I expected.
Instructor: It usually is. What day suits you?
Instructor: I have Tuesday mornings and Thursday evenings free at the moment.
Caller: Thursday evenings, please. Starting when?
Instructor: The twenty-fourth of April. I pick you up from home unless you'd rather meet somewhere.
Caller: Home is fine. Do I need to bring anything?
Instructor: Your provisional licence, every time — I can't teach you without seeing it, and that's the law rather than my rule. And glasses if you need them for reading a number plate.
Caller: Understood. What if I have to cancel?
Instructor: Forty-eight hours' notice and there's no charge. Less than that and it's half the lesson fee, because I can't fill the slot.

listeningScripts.title: Textile Museum Volunteer Induction
listeningScripts.text:
Curator: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming to the volunteer induction at the Harlow Textile Museum. I'm Sylvia, and I look after the volunteer programme.

Let me start with the collection, because it shapes everything else. Textiles are the most fragile category of object we hold. Light damages them permanently and cumulatively — there is no recovery — which is why the galleries are dimmer than visitors expect and why we rotate what is displayed rather than leaving favourites out. Expect to be asked why it is so dark several times a day, and the honest answer is that the alternative is not having the object at all in fifty years.

Handling: nobody handles objects in the first six months, and after that only with the collections team present. Cotton gloves are not used here, which surprises people — they reduce grip and cause drops, and clean dry hands are safer for most textiles.

Volunteering slots are Wednesday to Sunday, in half-days, and we ask for one half-day a week.

Now the building, which is easy to get lost in. The entrance hall has the desk straight ahead as you come in. The main gallery is on the ground floor to the left of that desk, running the length of the west side. The temporary exhibition space is on the right of the desk, on the east side, and it changes three times a year. Upstairs, the study room — where researchers look at objects by appointment — is directly above the entrance hall, and the conservation studio is next to it at the northern end of that floor, behind a door that stays locked. The shop is in the entrance hall itself, tucked to the left of the doors as you leave.

One request. If a visitor touches an object, do not seize their hand or raise your voice. Step alongside, say quietly that the oils in skin damage the fibres, and offer to show them the handling samples we keep for exactly that purpose. People touch things because they are interested, and an interested visitor is not someone to embarrass.

listeningScripts.title: Dividing a Group Report
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: So, the group report on the high street study. How have you split it?
Ade: We haven't, really. That's the problem — we've all been doing a bit of everything.
Bea: And we've got three versions of the introduction.
Tutor: How far through are you?
Ade: Two weeks left.
Tutor: Then stop working and spend an hour dividing it properly, because three people writing the same section is worse than two people writing nothing. Who is strongest on the data?
Bea: I am. I did the counts and the mapping.
Tutor: Then you write the results, and you own that section — nobody else edits it without telling you. Ade?
Ade: I've done most of the reading.
Tutor: Introduction and literature, same rule. And the third of you?
Ade: Kwame — he's been doing the interviews.
Tutor: Then he writes the discussion, because that is where the interviews earn their place. Now, the thing groups always get wrong: who writes the conclusion?
Bea: Whoever finishes first?
Tutor: No. One person writes it, at the end, after reading all three sections — and it is a different job from writing your own part. Decide now who that is.
Ade: What about consistency? Three people write differently.
Tutor: One person edits the whole thing in the last two days, for voice and for repetition. Not for content. If they start rewriting arguments you will end up back where you are now.
Bea: Should we set deadlines between us?
Tutor: Set them earlier than you think you need. Every group I have supervised has discovered a missing figure or an unreadable file on the last evening, and the groups that survive it are the ones that had two days of slack rather than none.

listeningScripts.title: How Food Labels Mislead
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Today I want to examine food labelling, and specifically why labels that are entirely truthful can still leave a shopper with a false impression.

Start with portion sizes, which do most of the work. Nutritional information is given per portion, and the portion is defined by the manufacturer, not by any external standard in most jurisdictions. A packet that a person would plausibly eat in one sitting may be labelled as two and a half portions, so the sugar figure printed on the front is divided by two and a half before anyone reads it. Nothing there is false. The impression created is nonetheless wrong.

The second mechanism is the comparative claim with an unstated baseline. "Thirty per cent less fat" invites the question: less than what? Sometimes it is less than the same manufacturer's previous formulation, sometimes less than a category average that includes unusually fatty products. The number is verifiable and the comparison is chosen.

Third, and most effective, are the claims that are true of the food and irrelevant to the decision. "No artificial colours" on a product whose issue is sugar content; "a source of fibre" on a biscuit; "made with real fruit" where the quantity is unstated. Each is accurate. Each also occupies the front of the pack, which is the only part most shoppers read, and each answers a question nobody was asking.

The response that works is not more information. Adding a fuller table to the back of the pack has been tested repeatedly and changes very little, because the constraint is attention rather than availability. What does change behaviour is simplification at the point of decision: front-of-pack schemes that rate a product overall, in colour, without requiring arithmetic. Purchases shift measurably where these are mandatory and barely at all where they are voluntary, because the products that would score badly simply decline to display them.

I want to end on the reason this matters beyond nutrition. We tend to treat honesty as a property of individual statements, and this is a case where every statement passes that test and the ensemble does not. Regulating for truthfulness sentence by sentence has been tried, works exactly as far as it is written, and leaves the impression untouched.
